q-80131:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=4 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=1\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={4}^{2}+{1}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =16+1 \\ {R}^{2} & =17 \\ R & =\sqrt{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

q-80126:
The sum formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\sqrt{7} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=3\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & =(\sqrt{7})^{2}+{3}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =7+9 \\ {R}^{2} & =16 \\ R & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

q-11295:
The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=3 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=2\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & =(2)^{2}+(3)^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =4+9 \\ {R}^{2} & =13 \\ R & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

q-124641:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u-v+1 \\ u-v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u-v \\ u-v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $T$ maps the boundary of $Δ$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $Δ,$ we find the images of each side.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/c89be48140d49ce8c9def44122aa2bfac779bdd02cfbfbe98f97d414a5637409.png)

          

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our square:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $b$ in each column:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The image of $u$ under $T$ is given by $Au+b.$ So, by applying $T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertices of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(1,1),(3,2),(1,0),$ and $(-1,-1).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/d038caec0aa360e5d8cc1bcb4a3aa4d88408496d947b312d47634e51bbf4a11f.png)

          

Finally, since $det(A)=-1<0,$ this transformation is not orientation-preserving.

q-124343:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation is already in matrix form 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $T$ maps the boundary of $Δ$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $Δ,$ we find the images of each side.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/5c38b3ccfc99ca173324e4caf4585e07991162c75741b20b5d288ce73ad0ff98.png)

             

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our triangle:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $b$ in each column:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The image of $u$ under $T$ is given by $Au+b.$ So, by applying $T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertices of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(0,1),(0,3),$ and $(-1,3).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/1bcadc0b9909159ebf99280e8d47d52891d2aa8653d9bc89bb2a3bb8363d4fb1.png)

          

Finally, since $det(A)=1>0,$ this transformation preserves orientation.
